title: Keynote: How Maintainers Can Build Their Way Through the AI Flood - Madelyn Olson & Jacob Murphy

segments.text: Good morning, everyone.
Um, my name is Agent Olson and this is
Agent Murphy. We've heard that agents
are very trendy these days, so thought
we'd come and play the part.
Um, and we're going to be talking a
little bit about how we in the Valkyrie
project are dealing with the significant
increase we've been seeing of AI-based
contributions.
So, obviously Valkyrie is not quite as
big as the Linux project, but we saw a
very similar trend to what Linus was
just talking about. Uh, so Valkyrie has
a 6-month release cycle. And over the
last 6 months, we've seen about a 55%
increase in the number of individual
commits that are coming to the project.
And now, some of these are good, great
commits from our existing contributor
base. Um, and some of them are, you
know, drive-by. We saw one that came
from someone we eventually identified as
just like an open claw bot. So, not
great quality contributions.
And this this is maybe tolerable.
But, the bigger trend we've noticed is
that the number of commits is the number
of lines of code inside those commits is
has seen a substantial increase. So,
we've seen about 500% increase in the
actual number of lines of code that we
have been receiving as maintainers.
Now, part of that is because AI tooling
has enabled the strong existing
committers of the project to build
really big, exciting, great things and
then contribute them to the project.
But, also we've seen that some of the
gen AI tooling really likes to write a
lot of code.
And that code is again not always the
highest quality.
And so, you know, both me and Jacob and
the other maintainers have been kind of
asked the question, "What do we do about
this?" And, um, the response that we
kind of keep hearing is just use agents.
And that's a response.
Um, it's not the most practical piece
useful piece of advice. And so, um,
we've been trying over the last 6
months, you know, we work for very, I'll
call them AI-forward companies who have
been encouraging us to use AI a lot. And
so we, you know, we're a little bit
ahead of this and we've been using AI in
tooling.
And so
we're going to try to share a little bit
of what we've been thinking about and
how we've been trying to apply it. We
know everyone's been, you know, taking
those agents and say, "Hey, just review
this code." And sometimes they're useful
feedback. But they oftentimes miss the
bigger picture. And, you know, I
actually just did a release of Valkyrie
9.1 yesterday. And yay! Thank you.
Um go try it out if you want it. It's
faster. It's better. But the kind of the
important thing is one of the things we
tried to do with this release was remove
a lot of the the toil that comes with
releasing.
And one of the things that I've noticed
and others have noticed is that using
agents and AI for automation only saves
time if you can really trust the end
results. So if we're using it to do
automated backporting, like we have to
actually trust that it's working.
Um when we do automated reviews, I end
up noticing that I still have to check
the results cuz although it finds bugs
and that's great, it still will
sometimes just add tests to the wrong
place. Or one of the things is we use
tickle, a very esoteric language for all
the testing in Valkyrie. And
a lot of the LLMs just don't really know
what to do with tickle. They'll write
new tests. They won't know what
abstractions are there.
And a lot of times a human still has to
go in and kind of fix all of that.
And so kind of
one of the things we've been trying very
hard is to build tooling that's at least
a combination of both exploiting the
non-determinism of AI and then pairing
it with the deterministic code we've
been writing.
So one of the specific things that we do
a lot of. So Valkyrie has a development
branch and that development branch is
where we write all the new code. And
then all of the individual commits get
ported from the development branch to
the individual releases. So I mentioned
we did 9.1 yesterday. And so one of the
tasks that need to be done was taking
all of the commits that are to be
backported and backport them to the
release branch.
Not the most exciting of jobs, but it's
actually something that AI has helped us
kind of do. So, we have a job that runs.
I think it currently runs once a day,
and it basically goes and collects all
of the pending commits.
It will then attempt to take all of
those commits one by one and apply them
individually onto the release branch.
So, in this case, you know, we found 46
candidates, and then we do, you know, a
chunk at a time cuz the end still is a
review that needs to happen.
So, some of these will apply very
cleanly. As long as a commit applies
cleanly and all the tests pass, we move
on.
And if we do find a commit, we can use
that and some use something like Cloud
Code to go and basically try to
uh fix it, right? Try to handle the
merge conflicts.
And then the end result is we have these
backporting PRs. So, at the end of all
of this, we still have a human in the
loop to be like, "Hey, were these all
cherry-picked correctly?" We have links
to all of the source PRs to make sure
um that you can actually trust the
providence of all this data. And then um
the latest version actually has more
details about the conflicts. Now, it
just says it's resolved, but you know,
we we're This is still a tool that we're
working on overall.
So, this is a combination of using AI
to do some of the toil that used to be
done by humans.
>> Yeah, and using AI isn't just for
backporting. We also I've been really
enjoying using the brand new Mythos
model to find bugs and vulnerabilities.

>> Uh
Mythos is classified.

4.6 then.
Uh so, we've been building uh
vulnerability and bug hunting harnesses.
Um Madeline and I actually both built
similar harnesses and came to the almost
the exact same results. Uh so, AI tends
to find similar bugs uh across multiple
runs. Uh and we've we've found over 20
different bugs using the system.
Uh additionally, you can we can run the
system proactively on unstable and find
the bugs before people are reporting
them to our project.
But not everything can be solved with
AI.
There's still a lot of automation where
AI isn't really the best tool that we
have.
AI itself is very non-deterministic and
there are
a lot of traditional deterministic
automations that still
need to be built for projects like
Valkyrie.
One of those cases was in verifying the
origin of code that is submitted to the
project.
We have a lot of use cases inside of
Valkyrie to identify and catch these uh
externally contributed commits that are
actually being pulled or ripped from
other similar projects that maybe have
different licenses.
And that creates copyright and legal
concerns for us.
So here we have a demo of this tool that
we built. We actually used AI to build
the tool,
but the tool itself is deterministic.
We've cloned here a PR that was actually
submitted to the Valkyrie repository
that we identified was
actually plagiarized from an external
project.
And here you can see that our automation
is running.
We call this our provenance guard. What
it's doing is it's comparing the changes
the hunks of lines of code that are
changed against a database of
pre-populated changes from those
external projects.
And you'll find out here soon that these
in this case the the hunks of code were
actually ripped and
this would prevent this code from being
merged, which will save us a bunch of
burden as maintainers where we would
previously have to scan this manually
and figure it out.
Um
And the goal here would be that then we
can rerun this
looks like
>> It's rerun.
>> rerun this check when when code is
submitted again and it should uh
successfully pass.
Um
Back to you.
>> It's running again. This is running in
real time, by the way. It does a lot of
you know, if you ask AI to do this, it
would take 45 minutes and spend 20,000
tokens.
>> I didn't see that.
>> Yeah, it's running. It's that little
tight spot. And see, it's successful.
And then we can go merge the PR if we
find that everything is, you know,
adequately with uh shown with adequate
provenance.
And the original takeaway that I wanted
to have from this brief keynote
was that at the end of the day, we still
want to make sure that maintainers are
the ones who are in charge of the
project direction, right? The
maintainers are the ones that have all
the context. They have all the history.
They know the individuals inside
organizations that are using these
projects and what, you know, what what's
actually needed and what's helping.
And the the comment that I mentioned
earlier, just like the just use agents.
One of the concerns I have is that
people are going to offload like the
reasoning, the thought behind the
projects to the agents and just say,
"Hey agent, what should we do about
this?"
And I don't think that's a good outcome.
I think there is something that gets
lost when we give too much over. Right?
When, you know, when something breaks at
2:00 in the morning, like the agent
might not be able to figure it out or
you might not have the person who has
the access to the right foundational
model to go and root cause it.
So, we really want to make sure that
these agents are being used to support
the existing maintainers of the project.
And I did just say this was the original
takeaway.
Cuz while I was being here and while I
was talking with others, I'm reminded
that, you know, the maintainers are
still human.
And, you know, I've seen so much more
burnout in the age of AI than I have in
quite a while.
So, for a long time I used to work on
Redis open source software, right? And
one of the frustrations I had the
project was that it was hard to
necessarily get all the code we wanted
to get in. And right now, you know, we
can write as much code as we want. Like
the Valkyrie project is vendor neutral.
We have all these tools that are
allowing us to write code faster than
ever. So, why are we feeling more burned
out than ever? And I think it's just
because of all of these expectations
that we're putting on top of
maintainers, and it's hard to sort of
keep up with that.
The number of, you know, pings that I've
gotten on our Slack and on GitHub about,
"Hey, we found this." The number of, you
know, security vulnerabilities we've
heard has gone up significantly. And
yes, people are providing patches.
Um and if they're they're they're
they're trying their best to do, you
know, to make our lives easier, but it
is still it's still difficult, right?
I'm spending significantly more time
both inside, you know, I I work at AWS.
I'm thankful that they let me spend my
time working on a great open source
project.
But it's still a huge amount of my time
outside of work to make sure this, you
know, this this launch happens. The 9.1
launch wasn't supposed to be last week.
It was supposed to be a week ago, but we
had so much stuff that needed to be
finalized and get working that it ended
up happening during this conference.
And so, I just want to everyone to take
away like, you know, I think maintainers
are under more stress than they've been
in a long time, and
you know, AI is a tool, as we've as
Linus said, as a lot of people have been
saying. And at the end of the day, the
tools should be helping them, right?
Helping with their mental health and
making sure they're able to continue to
maintain these maintain these projects
that we all depend immensely on.
So, that's the end of our talk. Um if
you want to see any of the tooling that
we sort of talked about, um there's a

GitHub. The project for the Providence

Valhalla project depends on
uh to continue running. Uh we're also

Uh if you have any questions, we'll also
